lessons.title: Characteristics of Living Things
lessons.objective: Separate living from non-living things using the seven life processes, and name the process a question describes.

content.heading: Characteristics of living things
paragraphs: A car moves, a crystal grows and a flame uses oxygen, yet none of them is alive. Biology separates living from non-living things by a set of processes that must all be present, not by any single sign.

content.heading: Seven processes that define life
paragraphs: A parked car can move, a crystal can grow and a flame can use up fuel. Each mimics one sign of life, which is why one sign cannot decide the question.

Living things carry out seven processes. Movement includes the whole body and the movement of substances inside it. Respiration releases energy from food. Nutrition obtains and uses food. Excretion removes metabolic waste. Growth is a permanent increase in size or cell number. Reproduction produces new individuals. Sensitivity, also called irritability, is the response to stimuli such as light, heat or touch.
Only a living thing performs all seven. A virus is a borderline case: it reproduces only inside a host cell and has no metabolism of its own.
bullets: All seven processes must be present; one alone proves nothing.
Movement includes internal transport, not only locomotion.
Growth in living things comes from cell division, not external addition.
content.takeaway: Life is the whole set of processes, never a single sign.

check.question: A crystal increases in size. Which characteristic does it imitate?
check.why: It looks like growth, but a crystal adds material on its outside; living growth is internal.

visual.caption: The same outward sign can have a different cause.

rows.right: Moved only by an outside force

content.heading: Nutrition and respiration
paragraphs: A green plant in sunlight and a boy eating rice both need energy, but they obtain it in opposite ways.

Nutrition is how an organism obtains and uses food. Autotrophs, such as green plants, make their own food by photosynthesis. Heterotrophs, such as humans, fungi and most bacteria, depend on ready-made food. Holozoic feeders ingest solid food, saprophytes absorb dissolved food from dead matter, and parasites feed on a living host.

Respiration is the breakdown of food to release energy. Aerobic respiration uses oxygen and releases carbon dioxide and water. Anaerobic respiration works without oxygen and releases less energy; in yeast it produces ethanol and carbon dioxide. Breathing is only the exchange of gases, not respiration itself.
bullets: An autotroph makes food; a heterotroph takes it ready-made.
Respiration releases energy; breathing only moves gases.
Anaerobic respiration yields less energy than aerobic respiration.
content.takeaway: Nutrition supplies the fuel; respiration releases its energy.

check.question: Which process releases energy from food inside a cell?
check.why: Respiration is the controlled breakdown of food that releases energy; breathing only exchanges gases.

content.heading: Excretion, reproduction and response
paragraphs: A student confuses sweating with passing faeces, and movement with responding to light. The exam tests exactly these boundaries.

Excretion removes waste made by metabolism, such as carbon dioxide, urea and excess salts. Egestion removes undigested food from the gut; it is not excretion because the material never entered the body's cells. Sweating is excretion of water and salts, while defecation is egestion.

Reproduction is the production of offspring. It is not needed for the survival of the individual, only for the species. Sensitivity, or irritability, is the response to a stimulus: a shoot bends towards light, a cockroach runs from a torch, and the pupil narrows in bright light.
bullets: Excretion removes metabolic waste; egestion removes undigested food.
Reproduction ensures the species, not the individual.
Sensitivity is a response to a stimulus.
content.takeaway: Name the process by its product, not by the organ that releases it.

check.question: Removal of undigested food from the alimentary canal is called
check.why: The food never entered the cells, so its removal is egestion, not excretion.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: When a question names an action, match it to the process that defines it: bending to light is sensitivity, shedding metabolic waste is excretion, and passing undigested food is egestion.

content.problem: A student argues that a burning candle is alive because it gives out heat and uses oxygen. Test the claim using the characteristics of living things.

steps.reason: Heat and oxygen use look like respiration, but respiration must release energy from food inside cells.
steps.result: The candle has no nutrition and no cells, so it cannot respire.
steps.predictPrompt: Which characteristic should you test first?

steps.reason: A candle does not grow from within and produces no metabolic waste.
steps.result: Growth and excretion are absent.

steps.reason: It cannot reproduce and does not respond to stimuli.
steps.result: Only one apparent sign remains.

steps.reason: Life requires the full set of processes, not one imitation.
steps.result: The candle is non-living.

content.question: A potted plant near a window bends its stem towards the light. Name the characteristic shown and explain why this is not locomotion.
hints: The plant is responding to a directional stimulus.
Locomotion is the movement of the whole organism from place to place.
The response is sensitivity, shown as positive phototropism.

lessons.title: Cell Structure and Function
lessons.objective: Identify the shared and distinguishing structures of plant and animal cells, and state the function of each organelle.

content.heading: Cell structure and function
paragraphs: Every living thing is built from cells, but plant and animal cells are not identical. Recognising the shared structures and the few differences is enough to answer most cell questions.

content.heading: What every cell shares
paragraphs: A cheek scraping and an onion epidermis look different under the microscope, yet both show the same basic machinery.

The cell membrane is a thin, selectively permeable layer that controls what enters and leaves. The cytoplasm is the jelly-like medium where reactions occur and organelles sit. The nucleus contains chromosomes made of DNA and controls the cell's activities. Mitochondria are the sites of aerobic respiration, releasing energy as ATP. Ribosomes build proteins from amino acids.
These five structures are enough to identify a cell as a cell. The membrane surrounds the cell, while the organelles work inside it.
bullets: The membrane controls exchange; the cytoplasm hosts reactions.
The nucleus holds DNA and controls activity.
Mitochondria release energy; ribosomes make protein.
content.takeaway: Membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondria and ribosomes are the shared kit.

check.question: Which organelle controls the cell's activities?
check.why: The nucleus contains the chromosomes that direct the cell.

content.heading: Plant and animal differences
paragraphs: A leaf cell and a liver cell both need energy, but only one of them can make its own food.

Plant cells have a cellulose cell wall outside the membrane, giving shape and support. They also contain chloroplasts with chlorophyll for photosynthesis, and a large permanent sap vacuole that stores water and salts and keeps the cell turgid.

Animal cells lack a cell wall and chloroplasts. They usually have small, temporary vacuoles, and centrioles that help in cell division. Both cell types have a membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondria and ribosomes.
bullets: Plant-only: cellulose wall, chloroplasts, large sap vacuole.
Animal-only: centrioles and small temporary vacuoles.
Both share the membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondria and ribosomes.
content.takeaway: The wall and chloroplasts are the plant give-aways.

check.question: Which structure is present in a plant cell but absent in an animal cell?
check.why: A cellulose cell wall surrounds plant cells; the membrane and organelles are shared.

visual.caption: Two shared kits, four separating features.

content.heading: Organelles that transport and package
paragraphs: A pancreas cell releases digestive enzymes. The protein must be built, moved, packaged and sent out without leaking into the cytoplasm.

Ribosomes on the rough endoplasmic reticulum make proteins. The rough ER transports them; the smooth ER makes lipids. The Golgi apparatus modifies, packages and secretes proteins, and lysosomes contain digestive enzymes that break down worn-out organelles and foreign material. Vacuoles store water, salts, pigments and waste.
The path of a secreted protein is ribosome, rough ER, Golgi, vesicle, membrane. A cell that secretes a lot, such as a pancreas cell, has many ribosomes and a large Golgi.
bullets: Rough ER makes and moves protein; smooth ER makes lipid.
The Golgi packages and secretes; lysosomes digest.
Secretory cells have many ribosomes and a large Golgi.
content.takeaway: Follow the protein: ribosome, ER, Golgi, vesicle, membrane.

check.question: Which organelle packages proteins for secretion?
check.why: The Golgi modifies and packages proteins into vesicles for release.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Never say the cell wall controls what enters. The wall is fully permeable and gives support; the membrane is the selectively permeable barrier.

content.problem: A microscope slide shows a cell with a cellulose wall, chloroplasts and a large vacuole. Name the cell type and state two structures it lacks that a liver cell would have.

steps.reason: A cellulose wall, chloroplasts and a large permanent vacuole are plant features.
steps.result: The cell is a plant cell.
steps.predictPrompt: Which features are shared by both cell types?

steps.reason: Animal cells have centrioles and small temporary vacuoles.
steps.result: These are the two structures to name.

steps.reason: Both cell types still have a membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondria and ribosomes.
steps.result: Do not list shared structures as differences.

steps.reason: Name only the structures the plant cell lacks.
steps.result: Centrioles and small temporary vacuoles.

content.question: A cell contains many mitochondria and a large Golgi apparatus. Suggest one job the cell might do and explain why it needs both features.
hints: Many mitochondria mean the cell uses a lot of energy.
A large Golgi means the cell secretes a lot of protein.
A muscle cell or a gland cell fits both clues.

lessons.title: Levels of Organisation
lessons.objective: Trace the sequence from cell to tissue, organ, system and organism, and place a named structure at the correct level.

content.heading: Levels of organisation
paragraphs: Life is built in steps: cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs form systems, and systems form the organism. Each step adds a new function, not just more cells.

content.heading: Cell and tissue
paragraphs: A single cell can live alone, but a human body needs groups of cells that do the same job.

The cell is the basic structural and functional unit. A tissue is a group of similar cells with a common origin, performing the same function. Epithelial tissue covers and protects surfaces; muscle tissue contracts; nervous tissue conducts impulses; connective tissue supports and binds.

Plants have tissues too: the epidermis covers the leaf, palisade mesophyll carries out photosynthesis, xylem transports water and phloem transports food. Hydra is often used to show the tissue level because its body wall is built mainly from two layers of tissue.
bullets: Cell: the basic unit of structure and function.
Tissue: similar cells with a shared job.
Examples: epithelium, muscle, nerve, xylem and phloem.
content.takeaway: A tissue is a team of similar cells with one job.

check.question: A group of similar cells performing the same function is a
check.why: Similar cells with a common function form a tissue.

content.heading: Organs and systems
paragraphs: A stomach is not just a bag of cells: it has muscle, glands and nerves, and it works with the mouth and intestines.

An organ is made of two or more tissues working together for a specific function. The leaf, root, heart, stomach, eye and kidney are organs. The onion bulb is a modified shoot and is used as the syllabus example of an organ.

A system is a group of organs working together on a major life process. The digestive system breaks down and absorbs food; the excretory system removes waste; the reproductive system produces offspring. A mammal also has circulatory, respiratory, nervous and skeletal systems.
bullets: Organ: two or more tissues with a specific job.
System: organs cooperating on a major process.
The leaf and the onion bulb are organs, not tissues.
content.takeaway: An organ combines tissues; a system combines organs.

check.question: Which of these is an organ?
check.why: A leaf contains epidermis, mesophyll and vascular tissues, so it is an organ.

content.heading: The full sequence
paragraphs: A euglena is one cell that swims, feeds and responds; a human is trillions of cells arranged into systems. Both are organisms.

The sequence is cell, tissue, organ, system, organism. In a unicellular organism such as Euglena, Paramecium or Chlamydomonas, one cell performs all life processes, so the cell and the organism are the same level. In multicellular organisms the levels are distinct.

Not every organism has every level. A hydra has tissues but no true organs or systems; a flowering plant has organs but no organ systems in the animal sense. The sequence is a ladder of increasing complexity, not a rule that every rung must appear.
bullets: Cell, tissue, organ, system, organism.
Unicellular organisms live at the cell level.
Hydra stops at tissues; plants have organs but no animal-style systems.
content.takeaway: Each level adds a function the level below cannot perform alone.

check.question: Which organism is unicellular?
check.why: Chlamydomonas is a single-celled green alga; the others are multicellular.

visual.caption: Each level is built from the one before it.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: To place a named structure, ask what it is made of. A leaf is made of tissues, so it is an organ; a stomach works with other organs, so it belongs to a system.

content.problem: Arrange these from simplest to most complex: stomach, epithelial cell, digestive system, epithelial tissue, human. Name each level.

steps.reason: The epithelial cell is the basic unit.
steps.result: 1. Cell.
steps.predictPrompt: Which structure is made of similar cells?

steps.reason: Epithelial cells form epithelial tissue.
steps.result: 2. Tissue.

steps.reason: The stomach contains epithelial, muscle and nervous tissue.
steps.result: 3. Organ.

steps.reason: The stomach works with the mouth, liver and intestines.
steps.result: 4. System.

steps.reason: The human is the complete living thing.
steps.result: 5. Organism.

content.question: A leaf is called an organ. Name two tissues it contains and explain why it is not a system.
hints: The leaf has an epidermis and palisade mesophyll.
It also has xylem and phloem in its veins.
A system is a group of organs, not a group of tissues.

lessons.title: The Five Kingdoms
lessons.objective: Place an organism in one of the five kingdoms, and explain the trend from a prokaryotic cell to specialised tissues and organs.

content.heading: The five kingdoms
paragraphs: A bacterium, a mushroom and a mango tree are all alive, but they are built on different plans. Biology sorts that variety into five kingdoms, then asks what each kingdom added to the basic unit of life: the cell.
The kingdoms are Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia. The order is not a family tree. It is a set of body plans, from cells without a nucleus to organisms with tissues, organs and systems.

content.heading: The first divide: nucleus or no nucleus
paragraphs: Every organism is made of cells, but not every cell is built the same way. A prokaryotic cell has no true nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles. Its DNA lies free in the cytoplasm, usually as a single circular chromosome. Bacteria and blue-green algae are prokaryotes, and they form the kingdom Monera.

All the other kingdoms are eukaryotic. Their cells have a true nucleus enclosed by a nuclear membrane, and compartments such as mitochondria, chloroplasts and a Golgi body. The nucleus is the first feature to check because it separates Monera from everything else.
bullets: Prokaryote: no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles.
Eukaryote: a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
Monera is the only prokaryotic kingdom.
content.takeaway: The first question in classification is whether the cell has a nucleus.

check.question: A cell has free circular DNA but no nuclear membrane. Which kingdom does it belong to?
check.why: Free circular DNA and no nucleus are prokaryotic features, which define Monera.

visual.caption: The nucleus is the first feature that separates the kingdoms.

content.heading: The five kingdoms at a glance
paragraphs: Monera contains bacteria and blue-green algae. Protista contains mainly single-celled eukaryotes such as Amoeba, Paramecium and Euglena. Fungi contains mushroom, Rhizopus and yeast. Plantae contains Spirogyra, mosses, ferns, cycads, maize and water leaf. Animalia contains Hydra, earthworms, insects, fish, frogs, birds and mammals.

Two further features separate them. Plants make their own food by photosynthesis and have cellulose cell walls. Fungi absorb ready-made food and have chitin cell walls. Animals ingest food and have no cell wall. Protists may be plant-like or animal-like, but they are not divided into tissues.
bullets: Monera: prokaryotic and mostly single-celled.
Protista: eukaryotic and mostly single-celled.
Fungi, Plantae and Animalia: eukaryotic and mostly multicellular.
content.takeaway: Name the kingdom from the cell plan and the way it feeds.

check.question: Which kingdom contains organisms with chitin cell walls and no chlorophyll?
check.why: Chitin walls and absorption of ready-made food are fungal features.

content.heading: What increasing complexity means
paragraphs: Complexity is not a single ladder, but the kingdoms do show a trend. A moneran is a prokaryotic cell with no nucleus. Protista is a single cell with a nucleus and organelles. Fungi and plants build bodies from many cells, and plants add tissues and organs. Animals add specialised tissues, organs and organ systems.

The trend is about division of labour. A Paramecium carries out all life processes in one cell. A maize plant has roots for absorption, leaves for photosynthesis and vascular tissue for transport. A mammal adds a heart, lungs, kidneys and a nervous system, each doing one job well.
bullets: More complexity means more cell types and more division of labour.
A single cell must carry out every life process itself.
Complexity is not the same thing as evolutionary superiority.
content.takeaway: Complexity is the number of specialised parts working together.

check.question: Which change most clearly shows increasing structural complexity?
options: Cells specialise into tissues and organs
check.why: Specialised tissues and organs are the structural step beyond a single cell.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Do not classify by colour or habitat. Euglena is green and swims, but it is a protist. Blue-green algae are photosynthetic, but they are bacteria. A mushroom is neither a plant nor an animal.

content.problem: A specimen is single-celled, green, has a nucleus and swims with a flagellum. A student calls it a plant. Correct the classification.

steps.reason: A true nucleus rules out Monera, whose cells have free DNA.
steps.result: The specimen is eukaryotic.
steps.predictPrompt: Which kingdom can you already rule out?

steps.reason: It is one cell, with no tissues or organs.
steps.result: It cannot be Plantae, which is multicellular with tissues.

steps.reason: Chloroplasts allow photosynthesis, but the flagellum and eyespot are protist features.
steps.result: It fits Euglena in Protista.

steps.reason: Kingdom is decided by cell plan and body plan, not colour.
steps.result: The specimen is a protist, not a plant.

content.question: A unicellular organism has no nucleus, a cell wall and a whip-like flagellum. Name its kingdom and explain why it cannot be a protist.
hints: Look for a nuclear membrane.
Protista is eukaryotic, so its cells have a true nucleus.
Monera is prokaryotic: free DNA and no membrane-bound organelles.

lessons.title: Monera and Protista
lessons.objective: Distinguish bacteria and blue-green algae from Amoeba, Paramecium and Euglena using the nucleus, nutrition and movement.

content.heading: Two kingdoms of small organisms
paragraphs: A drop of pond water can hold bacteria, blue-green algae, Amoeba, Paramecium and Euglena. They are all microscopic, but they belong to two different kingdoms. The difference is the nucleus, and it decides how each cell feeds, moves and reproduces.

content.heading: Monera: cells without a nucleus
paragraphs: Bacteria are the best-known monerans. Each is a single prokaryotic cell with a cell wall, a cell membrane and free circular DNA. Many have a capsule, and some have flagella for movement. They reproduce by binary fission, so one cell splits into two identical cells. Under harsh conditions, some form resistant endospores.

Blue-green algae, now called cyanobacteria, are also Monera. They contain chlorophyll and photosynthesise, but the pigment is not enclosed in a chloroplast. Some, such as Nostoc and Anabaena, fix nitrogen in rice fields. Bacteria decompose dead matter, cause disease, ferment food and supply antibiotics; cyanobacteria add nitrogen to the soil.
bullets: Binary fission, not mitosis, is the usual reproduction.
Cyanobacteria photosynthesise without chloroplasts.
Some bacteria fix nitrogen or form endospores.
content.takeaway: Monera is prokaryotic: no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles.

check.question: Why are blue-green algae placed in Monera and not in Plantae?
options: They are prokaryotic and have no chloroplasts
check.why: They photosynthesise, but their cells lack a nucleus and chloroplasts, so they are prokaryotes.

visual.caption: Both are microscopic, but only one has a nucleus.

content.heading: Protista: one cell with a nucleus
paragraphs: Protista are eukaryotes that are mostly single-celled. Amoeba moves and feeds with pseudopodia, flowing around food and engulfing it by phagocytosis. Paramecium is covered with cilia that beat in waves. An oral groove sweeps food into a food vacuole, and contractile vacuoles pump out excess water.

Euglena has a flagellum, a light-sensitive eyespot and chloroplasts. It photosynthesises in light but can absorb food in the dark, so it is mixotrophic. Protists reproduce mainly by binary fission, and Paramecium can exchange genetic material by conjugation. Contractile vacuoles also keep the cell from bursting in fresh water.
bullets: Amoeba: pseudopodia and phagocytosis.
Paramecium: cilia, oral groove and contractile vacuoles.
Euglena: flagellum, eyespot and chloroplasts.
content.takeaway: Protists are eukaryotic cells that live as a whole organism.

check.question: Which structure helps Paramecium move?
check.why: Paramecium is covered with cilia that beat in coordinated waves.

content.heading: Telling the two kingdoms apart
paragraphs: Start with the nucleus. If there is no nuclear membrane, the organism is Monera. If there is a true nucleus, it is eukaryotic. Then look at the organelles and the body. A protist has membrane-bound organelles and is usually a single cell.

Nutrition and movement are secondary clues. Euglena is green, but it is a protist, not a plant, because it is unicellular and has no tissues. Blue-green algae are green and photosynthetic, but they are bacteria because they have no nucleus or chloroplasts. Amoeba has no fixed shape, so a drawing of a round cell is not Amoeba.
bullets: Nucleus first; colour and habitat second.
Green does not mean plant.
A single cell with a nucleus is a protist, not Monera.
content.takeaway: Classify by the nucleus, then by organelles and body plan.

check.question: An organism is single-celled, has a nucleus and chloroplasts, and swims with a flagellum. What is it?
check.why: It is eukaryotic and unicellular, so it is a protist; plants are multicellular with tissues.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: A question may describe a green, motile cell and expect Euglena. Check the nucleus before you choose the kingdom, and check the organelles before you call it a plant.

content.problem: A pond sample contains two organisms. One has no nuclear membrane, a cell wall and a flagellum. The other has a nucleus, cilia and a contractile vacuole. Name the kingdom of each.

steps.operation: Test the first for a nucleus
steps.reason: No nuclear membrane means the DNA is free in the cytoplasm.
steps.result: The first organism is prokaryotic, so it belongs to Monera.
steps.predictPrompt: Which feature decides the kingdom before any other?

steps.operation: Test the second for a nucleus
steps.reason: A true nucleus makes it eukaryotic.
steps.result: The second organism is not Monera.

steps.reason: It is one cell with cilia and a contractile vacuole, which are protist features.
steps.result: The second organism is a protist, likely Paramecium.

steps.reason: A flagellum alone does not make an organism a protist; bacteria can have flagella too.
steps.result: The nucleus, not movement, separates the kingdoms.

content.question: A pond sample contains a green unicellular organism with a nucleus and a red eyespot. Name the organism and its kingdom, and explain why it is not a plant.
hints: The eyespot and flagellum point to a familiar protist.
A plant is multicellular and has tissues.
The organism is Euglena, in Protista.

lessons.title: Fungi
lessons.objective: Explain how fungi are built, how they feed and reproduce, and why they are neither plants nor animals.

content.heading: Fungi
paragraphs: A mushroom pushes through leaf litter after rain, and bread turns mouldy in a damp cupboard. Both are fungi, a kingdom that feeds by absorbing food rather than making it or swallowing it.

content.heading: The body of a fungus
paragraphs: A fungus is made of thread-like hyphae. A mass of hyphae is a mycelium, which spreads through soil, bread or dead wood. The cell wall is made of chitin, not cellulose, and the cells store carbohydrate as glycogen, not starch. Fungi have no chlorophyll, so they cannot photosynthesise.

Some fungi are unicellular, such as yeast. Most are multicellular, such as Rhizopus and mushrooms. The visible mushroom is only the fruiting body. Most of the organism is the mycelium hidden in the substrate. The fruiting body releases spores.
bullets: Hyphae make up the mycelium.
The cell wall is chitin and the storage carbohydrate is glycogen.
No chlorophyll means no photosynthesis.
content.takeaway: A fungus is a chitin-walled heterotroph built from hyphae.

check.question: A fungal cell wall is made mainly of
check.why: Fungi have chitin walls; plants have cellulose and bacteria have peptidoglycan.

visual.caption: A fungus looks plant-like but feeds like an animal.

content.heading: How fungi feed
paragraphs: Fungi are heterotrophs. Saprophytes, such as Rhizopus on bread and mushrooms on dead leaves, release enzymes onto the food and absorb the digested nutrients. Parasites feed on a living host and cause diseases such as ringworm and athlete's foot. Mutualists live with another organism and both benefit. Lichens are fungi with algae, and mycorrhizae are fungi with plant roots.

This extracellular digestion is why mould softens bread and why a mushroom appears on rotting wood. The fungus digests the substrate outside its body, then absorbs the soluble products. No food is taken in as solid particles.
bullets: Saprophyte: dead matter digested outside the body.
Parasite: feeds on a living host.
Mutualist: both partners benefit.
content.takeaway: Fungi digest food outside the body, then absorb it.

check.question: Rhizopus growing on bread is best described as
check.why: It releases enzymes onto dead bread and absorbs the products.

content.heading: Reproduction and importance
paragraphs: Fungi reproduce by spores. Rhizopus forms sporangia on upright stalks. When they burst, spores scatter and grow into new mycelia. A mushroom produces basidiospores on its gills. Yeast reproduces asexually by budding. Many fungi also have a sexual stage, which introduces variation.

Fungi are useful and harmful. Yeast ferments sugar in bread and brewing. Mushrooms are food. Penicillium yields penicillin. Fungi decompose dead matter and recycle nutrients. They also spoil food, cause crop diseases such as rust and smut, and cause human infections. Some mushrooms are poisonous.
bullets: Spores are the main dispersal unit.
Yeast buds; Rhizopus uses sporangia.
Fungi decompose, ferment, produce antibiotics and cause disease.
content.takeaway: Fungi recycle matter, but they also spoil food and cause disease.

check.question: Which fungus is used to produce an antibiotic?
check.why: Penicillium produces penicillin.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Mould on bread is Rhizopus, a saprophyte. Do not call it a plant because it is stationary. Look for chitin, glycogen and the absence of chlorophyll.

content.problem: A student says a mushroom is a plant because it does not move. Give three features that place it in Fungi.

steps.reason: Plant walls are cellulose; fungal walls are chitin.
steps.result: The wall points to Fungi.

steps.reason: A mushroom has no chlorophyll and cannot photosynthesise.
steps.result: It absorbs ready-made food, like a heterotroph.

steps.reason: The body is a mycelium of hyphae, not roots, stems and leaves.
steps.result: It has no plant organs.

steps.reason: Stationary does not mean plant.
steps.result: The mushroom belongs to Fungi.

content.question: Explain why a fungus cannot make its own food even when it grows in bright sunlight.
hints: Photosynthesis needs chlorophyll.
Fungi digest their food outside the body.
Saprophytes absorb the soluble products.

lessons.title: Plant Divisions
lessons.objective: Order Thallophyta, Bryophyta, Pteridophyta and Spermatophyta by vascular tissue, seeds and their dependence on water.

content.heading: Plant divisions
paragraphs: A moss, a fern and a mango tree all photosynthesise, but they solve the same problems differently. Plant divisions are grouped by how far each has moved from water, from a simple thallus to a seed that can be dispersed on land.

content.heading: Thallophyta and Bryophyta
paragraphs: Thallophyta have a thallus, a body that is not divided into true roots, stems and leaves. Spirogyra is a filamentous green alga that lives in fresh water. Its cells contain spiral chloroplasts and pyrenoids that store starch. It reproduces by fragmentation and conjugation.

Bryophyta include mosses and liverworts, such as Marchantia. They have rhizoids instead of true roots, no vascular tissue, and a dominant gametophyte generation. Their sperm must swim through a film of water to reach the egg, so they live in damp, shaded places and stay small.
bullets: Thallophyta: a thallus, with no true roots, stems or leaves.
Bryophyta: rhizoids, no vascular tissue, water needed for fertilisation.
Both are tied to damp habitats.
content.takeaway: Without vascular tissue, a plant cannot grow tall or far from water.

check.question: Which feature keeps mosses close to the ground?
check.why: Without xylem and phloem, mosses cannot transport water and food over long distances.

content.heading: Pteridophyta and Spermatophyta
paragraphs: Pteridophyta are ferns such as Dryopteris. They have true roots, stems and leaves, and vascular tissue of xylem and phloem, so they can grow taller than mosses. They still reproduce by spores and their sperm need water, so ferns are common in damp places.

Spermatophyta reproduce by seeds. Gymnosperms, such as cycads and conifers, bear naked seeds in cones. Angiosperms bear seeds enclosed in fruits. They flower and are divided into monocots, such as maize, and dicots, such as water leaf. Pollen carries the male gamete, so fertilisation no longer needs water.
bullets: Ferns: vascular tissue, spores, water for fertilisation.
Gymnosperms: naked seeds, usually in cones.
Angiosperms: flowers, fruits, monocots and dicots.
content.takeaway: The seed freed plants from standing water.

check.question: Which group produces seeds enclosed in fruits?
check.why: Angiosperms are flowering plants; their seeds develop inside fruits.

content.heading: The trend from water to land
paragraphs: The divisions show a series of innovations. Vascular tissue made tall growth possible. The seed protected the embryo and stored food. Pollen removed the need for swimming sperm. Flowers and fruits improved pollination and seed dispersal. Each step reduced dependence on water.

The trend is not a straight line from one living plant to another, and lower plants are not failures. Mosses and ferns still thrive in damp habitats. But the sequence explains why a mango tree can grow on dry land while a moss cannot. Each innovation widened the range of habitats a plant could occupy.
bullets: Vascular tissue solved transport.
Seeds and pollen solved reproduction on land.
Flowers and fruits improved dispersal.
content.takeaway: Each plant division removes one more dependence on water.

check.question: Which innovation first allowed plants to reproduce without water?
check.why: Pollen carries the male gamete, so fertilisation does not need a film of water.

visual.caption: One innovation at a time, from water to land.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Match the example to the division: Spirogyra is Thallophyta, Marchantia is Bryophyta, Dryopteris is Pteridophyta, and maize is an angiosperm.

content.problem: A plant has vascular tissue, true leaves and spores, but no seeds. It grows in damp shade. Name its division and explain why it still needs water.

steps.reason: Xylem and phloem rule out Thallophyta and Bryophyta.
steps.result: The plant is either Pteridophyta or Spermatophyta.

steps.reason: Spores instead of seeds point to Pteridophyta.
steps.result: The plant is a fern, such as Dryopteris.

steps.reason: Fern sperm must swim through a film of water to reach the egg.
steps.result: Fertilisation ties the fern to damp shade.

steps.reason: Vascular tissue allows height, but reproduction still needs water.
steps.result: The plant is a pteridophyte.

content.question: A farmer wants a tall crop on dry land. Explain why an angiosperm is better suited than a moss or a fern.
hints: Compare vascular tissue first.
Then compare how each plant fertilises and disperses its young.
Seeds and pollen remove the need for a film of water.

lessons.title: Plant Life Spans
lessons.objective: Classify a plant as an annual, biennial or perennial from its life cycle, and give Nigerian examples of each.

content.heading: Plant life spans
paragraphs: A maize field is harvested and cleared within one season, while a mango tree fruits for decades. Both are flowering plants. Their difference is the span of their life cycle, and that difference decides how a farmer plants, harvests and stores seed.

content.heading: Annuals: one season, one generation
paragraphs: An annual completes its life cycle within one growing season or year. It germinates, grows, flowers, forms fruit and seed, and then dies. Maize, rice, cowpea and sunflower are annuals; tomato is usually grown as an annual. The whole plant dies after seeds are formed, so the species survives only as seed.

Farmers like annuals because the cycle is short and predictable. They can plant two or three crops a year where water and soil allow, and they can rotate cereals with legumes. The cost is that the field must be replanted every season, and the soil is bare between crops.
bullets: An annual completes its life cycle in one season, then dies.
Nigerian examples include maize, rice, cowpea and tomato.
Survival depends on seed, so seed storage matters.
content.takeaway: An annual spends everything on one generation of seed.

check.question: Which of these is an annual crop?
check.why: Maize germinates, flowers, sets seed and dies within one season.

content.heading: Biennials: two years, one seed crop
paragraphs: A biennial grows vegetatively in its first year, storing food in roots, stems or leaves. In the second year it uses that store to flower, fruit, set seed and die. Carrot, onion, cabbage, beet and turnip are common biennials. The edible part is usually the first-year storage organ.

Cold treatment, or vernalisation, often triggers flowering in the second year. A young plant exposed to cold early may flower in its first year and lose its market value. A gardener who wants seed must leave the plant through the second season.
bullets: Year one: vegetative growth and food storage.
Year two: flowering, seed production and death.
Vernalisation often triggers the second-year flower.
content.takeaway: A biennial stores food first, then spends it on one seed crop.

check.question: A carrot plant flowers and sets seed in its second year. It is
check.why: It grows vegetatively in year one and reproduces in year two before dying.

content.heading: Perennials: many years, repeated fruiting
paragraphs: A perennial lives for more than two years and usually flowers and fruits many times. Mango, orange, cashew, oil palm, cocoa and most grasses are perennials. Some lose their leaves in the dry season and regrow; others stay evergreen. A few, such as bamboo, flower once and die after many years, so perennial describes the lifespan, not a guarantee of repeated flowering.

Perennials invest in permanent structures: woody stems, deep roots and food reserves. They protect the soil, provide shade and give repeated harvests, but they take years to mature and cannot be shuffled with the seasons like annuals.
bullets: A perennial lives more than two years and usually fruits repeatedly.
Nigerian examples include mango, cashew, oil palm and cocoa.
Woody stems and deep roots are long-term investments.
content.takeaway: A perennial spreads its reproduction over many seasons.

check.question: Which set contains only perennials?
check.why: Mango, cashew and oil palm live and fruit for many years.

visual.caption: An annual completes this cycle in one season, then dies.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: A biennial does not live two years and then fruit for years. It dies after its second-year seed crop. Carrot and onion are biennials; mango and oil palm are perennials.

content.problem: A farmer plants carrot in year one and sees only leaves. In year two the plant flowers, sets seed and dies. Classify the plant and explain what changed.

steps.reason: The plant grows in year one and reproduces in year two.
steps.result: It has a two-year life cycle.
steps.predictPrompt: Which class completes its cycle in one season?

steps.reason: The carrot root is a food store, not a seed crop.
steps.result: Year one is vegetative growth.

steps.reason: Cold treatment, or vernalisation, prepares the plant to flower.
steps.result: The stored food supports the second-year flower.

steps.reason: The plant dies after one seed crop in its second year.
steps.result: Carrot is a biennial.

content.question: A student calls maize a perennial because it is planted every year. Correct the statement and give two differences between maize and mango.
hints: Being replanted every year is not the same as living for many years.
Maize completes its life cycle in one season and dies.
Mango has a woody stem and fruits repeatedly over many years.

lessons.title: Invertebrate Phyla
lessons.objective: Order the six named invertebrate phyla by symmetry, body cavity and segmentation, and identify their examples.

content.heading: Invertebrate phyla
paragraphs: More than nine in ten animals have no backbone. The syllabus names six invertebrate phyla, and each adds a body-plan feature that the next group builds on: symmetry, a body cavity, segmentation and jointed limbs.

content.heading: Coelenterata and Platyhelminthes
paragraphs: Coelenterata, also called Cnidaria, include Hydra and jellyfish. They have radial symmetry, two cell layers, a single opening to a gastrovascular cavity, and tentacles with stinging cells called nematocysts. Hydra lives in fresh water and can regenerate from a fragment.

Platyhelminthes are flatworms such as Taenia, the tapeworm. They have bilateral symmetry, a flattened body, no body cavity and no true segments. Taenia lives in the intestine of a vertebrate host, attaches with hooks and suckers, and absorbs digested food through its body surface. Its life cycle needs two hosts.
bullets: Coelenterata: radial symmetry, two layers, one opening.
Platyhelminthes: bilateral, flattened and with no body cavity.
Taenia is a parasite with hooks and suckers.
content.takeaway: The first invertebrate steps are symmetry and a fixed body plan.

check.question: Which feature is characteristic of Hydra?
check.why: Hydra is a coelenterate with radial symmetry and stinging tentacles.

content.heading: Nematoda and Annelida
paragraphs: Nematoda are roundworms such as Ascaris. They have bilateral symmetry, a cylindrical unsegmented body, a tough cuticle and a pseudocoelom, a body cavity not fully lined by mesoderm. Ascaris lives in the small intestine and produces large numbers of eggs that pass out in faeces.

Annelida are segmented worms such as the earthworm. They have a true coelom, a closed circulatory system, setae for grip and a body divided into repeating segments. Segmentation allows different regions to specialise. The earthworm burrows through soil, aerating it and mixing organic matter into it.
bullets: Nematoda: round, unsegmented, cuticle and pseudocoelom.
Annelida: segmented, true coelom and setae.
Earthworms improve soil structure and fertility.
content.takeaway: Segmentation and a true coelom are the annelid advance.

check.question: Which feature separates Annelida from Nematoda?
options: A segmented body with a true coelom
check.why: Annelids are segmented and have a true coelom; nematodes are unsegmented with a pseudocoelom.

content.heading: Arthropoda and Mollusca
paragraphs: Arthropoda have a hard exoskeleton of chitin, jointed appendages and a segmented body. They include insects, crustaceans, arachnids and millipedes. The exoskeleton protects the body but must be shed by moulting for growth. Arthropoda is the largest phylum. It contains more species than all the other animal phyla combined.

Mollusca have a soft unsegmented body, a muscular foot, a mantle and usually a shell. Snails, slugs, clams and octopuses are molluscs. The mantle secretes the shell, and the radula is a rasping tongue used for feeding. Snails live in damp places on land and in water.
bullets: Arthropoda: exoskeleton, jointed legs and moulting.
Mollusca: soft body, mantle, muscular foot and shell.
Arthropoda is the largest animal phylum.
content.takeaway: Jointed limbs and a mantle mark the two largest invertebrate groups.

check.question: A snail belongs to
check.why: Snails have a soft body, a mantle and a shell, which are mollusc features.

visual.caption: Two successful body plans: jointed outside, soft inside a shell.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Do not call every worm an annelid. Taenia is a flatworm, Ascaris is a roundworm, and the earthworm is the segmented annelid.

content.problem: A specimen has a soft body, a shell and a muscular foot. Another has jointed legs and a chitin exoskeleton. Name the phylum of each.

steps.reason: A soft body with a mantle and shell points to Mollusca.
steps.result: The first specimen is a mollusc, such as a snail.
steps.predictPrompt: Which phylum has a chitin exoskeleton?

steps.reason: Jointed legs and a chitin exoskeleton are arthropod features.
steps.result: The second specimen is an arthropod.

steps.reason: A shell is secreted by the mantle; an exoskeleton is shed by moulting.
steps.result: The two phyla solve support differently.

steps.reason: Body covering and appendages decide the phylum.
steps.result: The specimens are Mollusca and Arthropoda.

content.question: Explain why segmentation is an advance over a solid, unsegmented body. Use the earthworm and a flatworm in your answer.
hints: Segments can carry different organs and appendages.
A true coelom gives space for organs and a hydrostatic skeleton.
A flatworm has a flattened body with no body cavity.

lessons.title: Insects and Their Importance
lessons.objective: Describe the insect body plan, distinguish complete from incomplete metamorphosis, and assess insects' economic and environmental importance.

content.heading: Insects and their importance
paragraphs: Insects are arthropods with three body regions, six legs and usually two pairs of wings. They are the most numerous animals on land, and JAMB tests both their body plan and their mixed value to people.

content.heading: The insect body plan
paragraphs: An insect has three body regions: head, thorax and abdomen. The head carries a pair of antennae, compound eyes and mouthparts. The thorax has three pairs of jointed legs and usually two pairs of wings. The abdomen contains the digestive and reproductive organs. Breathing is through spiracles and tracheae, not lungs.

The exoskeleton is made of chitin. It protects the insect and reduces water loss, but it cannot stretch, so the insect must moult to grow. Insects have an open circulatory system, with haemolymph pumped by a dorsal heart. Their small size and tracheal system limit them to relatively short diffusion paths.
bullets: Head, thorax and abdomen; three pairs of legs.
Spiracles and tracheae carry air directly to the tissues.
The chitin exoskeleton must be moulted for growth.
content.takeaway: An insect is a three-part arthropod with six legs and tracheal breathing.

check.question: Which structure is found on the thorax of an insect?
check.why: The thorax bears the legs and wings; the head bears antennae and mouthparts.

content.heading: Complete and incomplete metamorphosis
paragraphs: Metamorphosis is the change in body form between the young and the adult. In complete metamorphosis the insect passes through four stages: egg, larva, pupa and adult. Butterflies, mosquitoes, houseflies, bees and beetles do this. The larva is often a feeding machine, while the adult specialises in reproduction and dispersal.

In incomplete metamorphosis there are only three stages: egg, nymph and adult. The nymph resembles the adult but is smaller and has no wings or only wing buds. Cockroaches, grasshoppers, termites and dragonflies do this. There is no pupal stage, and the nymph moults repeatedly.
bullets: Complete: egg, larva, pupa and adult.
Incomplete: egg, nymph and adult.
The pupa is the stage that separates the two patterns.
content.takeaway: Count the stages: four means complete, three means incomplete.

check.question: A cockroach hatches as a small wingless form that resembles its parent. This is
check.why: Egg, nymph and adult are the three stages of incomplete metamorphosis.

visual.caption: The pupa is the extra stage in complete metamorphosis.

content.heading: Economic and environmental importance
paragraphs: Insects are useful. Bees, wasps and butterflies pollinate crops and wild plants. Bees give honey and wax; silkworms give silk; lac insects give shellac. Insects are food for birds, fish and reptiles, and some feed on pests as biological control agents. They decompose dung and dead matter, recycling nutrients.

Insects are also harmful. Locusts and armyworms destroy crops; weevils and beetles damage stored grain; aphids suck sap and transmit plant viruses. Mosquitoes transmit malaria, yellow fever and dengue; tsetse flies transmit sleeping sickness; houseflies carry typhoid and cholera organisms. The same insect can be useful at one stage and harmful at another.
bullets: Pollination, honey, silk, wax and biological control.
Crop pests and stored-product pests.
Vectors of malaria, sleeping sickness and typhoid.
content.takeaway: Judge an insect by its stage, its numbers and its role in the food web.

check.question: Which insect is a vector of malaria?
check.why: The female Anopheles mosquito transmits the Plasmodium parasite when it bites.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: A butterfly is harmful as a larva and useful as an adult pollinator. Read the stage named in the question before deciding harmful or useful.

content.problem: A farmer finds caterpillars stripping leaves and adult butterflies visiting flowers. Are the insects harmful or useful? Explain.

steps.reason: The caterpillar is the larval stage; the butterfly is the adult.
steps.result: The same species is present at two stages.

steps.reason: Caterpillars have chewing mouthparts and eat leaves.
steps.result: The larval stage damages the crop.

steps.reason: The adult visits flowers for nectar and transfers pollen.
steps.result: The adult stage pollinates crops.

steps.reason: The answer depends on the stage named in the question.
steps.result: The insect is both harmful and useful.

content.question: Name one insect that is useful in one stage and harmful in another, and explain the difference.
hints: Think of a butterfly or a moth.
The larva usually feeds on leaves.
The adult may pollinate flowers.

lessons.title: Vertebrate Classes
lessons.objective: Compare Pisces, Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves and Mammalia by skin, respiration, reproduction and heart, and trace the move from water to land.

content.heading: Vertebrate classes
paragraphs: A fish, a frog, a lizard, a bird and a goat all have a backbone, but each solves the problems of support, breathing and reproduction differently. The five vertebrate classes show a step-by-step move from water to land.

content.heading: Pisces and Amphibia
paragraphs: Pisces are fish. They have a streamlined body, scales, fins and gills. Cartilaginous fish, such as sharks and rays, have a skeleton of cartilage; bony fish, such as tilapia and catfish, have a bony skeleton. Most fish reproduce by external fertilisation, releasing eggs and sperm into water, and their heart has two chambers.

Amphibia include frogs and toads. Their moist, scale-less skin allows gas exchange, and they also have lungs. They lay jelly-covered eggs in water, and the young tadpole has gills and a tail. Metamorphosis changes the tadpole into an air-breathing adult. Amphibians have a three-chambered heart and still depend on water for reproduction.
bullets: Pisces: gills, fins, scales, external fertilisation and a two-chambered heart.
Amphibia: moist skin, lungs, eggs in water and a three-chambered heart.
Amphibians are the bridge between water and land.
content.takeaway: Amphibians breathe air but still return to water to breed.

check.question: Which feature ties a frog to water for reproduction?
check.why: Frog eggs dry out on land, and the tadpole stage is aquatic.

content.heading: Reptilia and Aves
paragraphs: Reptilia include lizards, snakes, turtles and crocodiles. They have dry skin covered with scales, and they breathe with lungs. Their eggs have leathery or hard shells that resist drying, and fertilisation is internal, so reptiles can breed on land. They are ectothermic, using the environment to regulate body temperature. Most have a three-chambered heart, but crocodiles have four.

Aves are birds. They have feathers, a beak, wings and hollow bones. Their heart has four chambers, and they are endothermic, generating their own heat. Birds lay hard-shelled eggs and incubate them. Their lungs connect to air sacs, which make gas exchange efficient for flight. Birds have no teeth; the beak is shaped for the diet.
bullets: Reptilia: dry scales, shelled eggs, internal fertilisation and ectothermy.
Aves: feathers, beak, four-chambered heart and endothermy.
Shelled eggs freed both groups from breeding in water.
content.takeaway: The shelled egg is the reptile and bird answer to life on dry land.

check.question: Which feature is shared by reptiles and birds?
check.why: Both groups fertilise internally and lay eggs with shells that resist drying.

visual.caption: The pivotal step: an egg that can survive out of water.

content.heading: Mammalia and the move to land
paragraphs: Mammalia include humans, cows, goats, bats and whales. They have hair or fur, mammary glands that produce milk, a diaphragm and a four-chambered heart. Most give birth to live young and care for them. Mammals are endothermic and have differentiated teeth for different diets.

The vertebrate classes show a trend. Gills give way to lungs, external fertilisation to internal fertilisation, jelly eggs to shelled eggs, and cold-bloodedness to warm-bloodedness. Each change reduces dependence on water. The trend is not a straight line, and each class still has adaptations to its own habitat.
bullets: Mammalia: hair, mammary glands, milk and a four-chambered heart.
Trend: gills to lungs, external to internal fertilisation, jelly to shelled eggs.
Each class remains adapted to its own habitat.
content.takeaway: Vertebrates moved onto land by changing how they breathe, breed and control heat.

check.question: Which set of features is unique to mammals?
check.why: Hair and mammary glands are defining mammalian features.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Cold-blooded means ectothermic, not always cold. A lizard on a hot rock has a high body temperature; it gains heat from the environment.

content.problem: A vertebrate has dry scales, lays shelled eggs on land and breathes with lungs. Name its class and one reason it is not an amphibian.

steps.reason: Dry scales and shelled eggs are reptile features.
steps.result: The animal belongs to Reptilia.
steps.predictPrompt: Which class has moist, scale-less skin?

steps.reason: Internal fertilisation and a shelled egg allow breeding on land.
steps.result: The animal does not need water to reproduce.

steps.reason: Amphibians lay jelly-covered eggs in water and have a larval stage.
steps.result: The animal has no aquatic larval stage.

steps.reason: Skin, egg and life cycle all point one way.
steps.result: The vertebrate is a reptile, not an amphibian.

content.question: Explain why a frog must return to water to breed while a lizard does not.
hints: Compare the egg coverings.
Compare where fertilisation happens.
A frog has an aquatic tadpole; a lizard hatches as a miniature adult.
